culturalTips: In Japan, it's considered polite to slurp your noodles — it shows you're enjoying the meal and even helps cool it down. In Italy, the same sound at the table would raise eyebrows.
Italians greet close friends and family with a kiss on both cheeks, starting from the right. In Japan, a slight bow is the more common greeting, even among friends.

Punctuality carries different weight in each culture: in Japan, arriving even a minute late is unusual and can seem disrespectful. In Italy, arriving 10-15 minutes late to a casual gathering is often completely normal.

Gift-giving in Japan is a careful ritual — gifts are often wrapped elaborately and given with both hands. In Italy, gifts are usually more casual, but never bring an odd number of flowers unless it's chrysanthemums, which are reserved for funerals.

grammar.comingSoonTitle: Grammar lessons are on the way
grammar.comingSoonDesc: Structured grammar paths for Italian and Japanese are in development.

lessons.it1Desc: Italian nouns are either masculine or feminine. Masculine nouns often end in -o (il libro), feminine ones in -a (la casa). Articles and adjectives must match: il libro rosso, la casa rossa.
lessons.it2Desc: Regular verbs fall into three groups by ending: -are (parlare), -ere (vedere), -ire (dormire). Each has its own set of endings for io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi, loro.
lessons.it3Desc: "Essere" (to be) and "avere" (to have) are the two most important verbs, used both alone and to build compound tenses like the passato composto.
lessons.it4Desc: Most nouns change their final vowel to form the plural: -o and -e become -i (libro → libri, chiave → chiavi), -a becomes -e (casa → case).
lessons.ja1Desc: Japanese sentences follow Subject-Object-Verb order, unlike Italian's Subject-Verb-Object. "Watashi wa sushi wo tabemasu" literally means "I sushi eat."
lessons.ja2Desc: Particles mark the role of each word. は (wa) marks the topic, が (ga) marks the subject, を (wo) marks the object of a verb.
lessons.ja3Desc: Verbs have a polite form (desu/masu, used with strangers or in formal settings) and a plain form (used with close friends and family).
lessons.ja4Desc: Japanese nouns don't change for singular/plural or gender — "neko" means both "cat" and "cats", context tells you which.
